subject: Corporate and Other Laws
question_html: Under section 2(16) of the Companies Act, 2013, how is the term 'charge' defined?

options.A: An interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both, as security, and includes a mortgage
options.B: A charge means exclusively a mortgage registered under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and does not extend to any other form of interest or lien created as security
options.C: A charge means any unsecured borrowing by a company, whether or not backed by an interest or lien on the company's property or assets
options.D: A charge means only a lien created on the company's current, fluctuating assets such as stock-in-trade, and excludes any interest created on fixed, permanent assets

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) An interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company or any of its undertakings or both, as security, and includes a mortgage

Section 2(16) defines 'charge' as an interest or lien created on the property or assets of a company (or any of its undertakings, or both) as security - and this definition expressly includes a mortgage, making the term wider than mortgage alone.

question_html: Under section 77, the property or assets charged may be 'tangible' assets or 'otherwise' - what does this signify, and does a charge created by deposit of title deeds also require registration?

options.A: The word 'otherwise' narrows the scope of the provision to exclude intangible assets entirely, and a charge created by deposit of title deeds is exempt from registration since no formal mortgage deed is executed
options.B: The word 'otherwise' widens the scope of the provision to cover intangible assets as well, such as a patent, copyright, or trademark; and a charge created by deposit of title deeds (a mode banks often use instead of a formal mortgage) is also registrable by the borrowing company
options.C: The word 'otherwise' has no interpretive effect at all on the scope of section 77, and only charges created by a registered mortgage deed require registration
options.D: The word 'otherwise' widens the scope only to cover financial assets like shares or debentures, while a charge by deposit of title deeds remains permanently unregistrable

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) The word 'otherwise' widens the scope of the provision to cover intangible assets as well, such as a patent, copyright, or trademark; and a charge created by deposit of title deeds (a mode banks often use instead of a formal mortgage) is also registrable by the borrowing company

The word 'otherwise' has the effect of widening the scope and operation of the provision, bringing intangible assets (patent, copyright, trademark) within the ambit of registrable charges, in addition to tangible assets (land, buildings, machinery) and financial assets (investment in shares/debentures). A charge created by deposit of title deeds under section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 is also registrable by the borrowing company.

question_html: In what circumstance does the Companies Act, 2013 require a charge to be compulsorily registered under Chapter VI?

options.A: Only where the company borrows money exclusively from a bank (and not from any other financial institution or person), and only for working capital loans, not term loans
options.B: Only where the loan amount exceeds rupees one crore, this monetary threshold being a precondition for compulsory registration under Chapter VI
options.C: Whenever a company borrows money (by way of term loans, working capital loans, or otherwise) from financial institutions, banks, or any other person, by offering its property or assets (or any of its undertakings) as security, a charge is created on such property/assets in favour of the lender, and such a charge is compulsorily registrable under Chapter VI
options.D: Only where the security offered consists of immovable property; charges over movable or intangible property are exempted from compulsory registration under Chapter VI

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Whenever a company borrows money (by way of term loans, working capital loans, or otherwise) from financial institutions, banks, or any other person, by offering its property or assets (or any of its undertakings) as security, a charge is created on such property/assets in favour of the lender, and such a charge is compulsorily registrable under Chapter VI

Whenever a company borrows money by way of loans (term loans, working capital loans, or otherwise) from financial institutions, banks, or any other person, by offering its property/assets/undertakings as security, a charge arises in favour of the lender, and Chapter VI (along with the Companies (Registration of Charges) Rules, 2014) makes such a charge compulsorily registrable - irrespective of the lender's category, the loan amount, or whether the security is movable, immovable, tangible, or intangible.

question_html: What are the distinguishing features of a 'fixed charge', and can the borrowing company freely sell an asset subject to a fixed charge?

options.A: A fixed charge is created on assets of a fluctuating nature, identified only at the time of the company's liquidation rather than at the time of creation of the charge, and can be freely sold by the company at any time without the charge-holder's consent
options.B: A fixed charge is created on specific, permanent assets, but the company may freely sell such assets at any time without the charge-holder's consent, provided it informs the charge-holder in writing within 30 days of the sale
options.C: A fixed charge automatically converts into a floating charge upon creation, and thereafter behaves identically to a floating charge for all purposes, including the company's freedom to deal with the charged asset
options.D: A fixed charge is created on specific assets of a permanent nature (such as land, buildings, or machinery), identified at the time of creation of the charge; the borrowing company may use such assets but cannot sell them during the period of the charge except with the permission or consent of the charge-holder, and the charge is vacated only when the borrowed money is repaid in full

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) A fixed charge is created on specific assets of a permanent nature (such as land, buildings, or machinery), identified at the time of creation of the charge; the borrowing company may use such assets but cannot sell them during the period of the charge except with the permission or consent of the charge-holder, and the charge is vacated only when the borrowed money is repaid in full

A fixed charge attaches to specific, identified assets of a permanent nature (land, buildings, machinery, office premises) - usually created by mortgage or deposit of title deeds. The company may use such assets but cannot sell them during the charge period without the charge-holder's permission/consent, and the charge is vacated only upon full repayment of the borrowed money - as illustrated by Pearl Electronics Limited's term loan secured against its office building.

question_html: What are the distinguishing features of a 'floating charge', and what happens when the company deals with the charged assets (e.g., stock-in-trade) in the ordinary course of business?

options.A: A floating charge is created on assets or a class of assets of a fluctuating/changing nature (such as raw material, stock-in-trade, or debtors), both present and future; the borrowing company is permitted to use, sell, or otherwise deal with such assets in the ordinary course of its business, and a buyer of such assets acquires them free of the charge
options.B: A floating charge is created only on specific, permanently identified assets such as land and buildings, and the borrowing company is prohibited from dealing with such assets in any manner without the charge-holder's prior written consent
options.C: A floating charge attaches immediately and permanently to each individual unit of stock-in-trade from the moment of its creation, such that a buyer purchasing any item of stock takes it subject to the charge
options.D: A floating charge can only be created over a company's cash and bank balances, and never over physical assets such as raw material, stock-in-trade, or debtors

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) A floating charge is created on assets or a class of assets of a fluctuating/changing nature (such as raw material, stock-in-trade, or debtors), both present and future; the borrowing company is permitted to use, sell, or otherwise deal with such assets in the ordinary course of its business, and a buyer of such assets acquires them free of the charge

A floating charge is created on a class of fluctuating assets (raw material, stock-in-trade, debtors, etc.), both present and future - it 'floats' above ever-changing assets, and the company may deal with them (sell, use in manufacture, etc.) in the ordinary course of business, with the buyer taking the asset free of the charge - as illustrated by the retail showroom and Smart Shoes Limited examples in the Study Material.

question_html: What is the core distinction between a fixed charge and a floating charge, in terms of the assets covered and the company's freedom to deal with them?

options.A: There is no substantive distinction between a fixed charge and a floating charge; the two terms are simply alternative names for the identical legal concept under section 2(16)
options.B: A fixed charge attaches to specific, identified assets of a permanent nature, restricting the company's ability to deal with (particularly, sell) them without the charge-holder's consent; a floating charge attaches to a class of fluctuating assets (present and future) with which the company remains free to deal in the ordinary course of business, until the charge crystallises
options.C: A fixed charge is always unsecured, whereas a floating charge is always fully secured by a registered mortgage over identified immovable property
options.D: A fixed charge can be created only by a private company, whereas a floating charge can be created only by a public company, this being a company-type-based (rather than asset-based) distinction

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) A fixed charge attaches to specific, identified assets of a permanent nature, restricting the company's ability to deal with (particularly, sell) them without the charge-holder's consent; a floating charge attaches to a class of fluctuating assets (present and future) with which the company remains free to deal in the ordinary course of business, until the charge crystallises

The core distinction lies in the nature of the assets and the company's dealing freedom: a fixed charge fastens onto specific, identified, permanent assets (restricting dealings without consent), while a floating charge hovers over a changing class of assets (raw material, stock, debtors) with which the company may freely deal in the ordinary course of business - until the floating charge crystallises into a fixed charge.

question_html: What is meant by 'crystallization' of a floating charge, and in what state does a floating charge remain until crystallization occurs?

options.A: Crystallization occurs automatically on the very date the floating charge is first created, immediately converting it into a fixed charge from inception, with no dormant period at all
options.B: Crystallization occurs only when the company voluntarily converts the floating charge into a fixed charge by a Board resolution, and cannot occur due to any default or liquidation event
options.C: Crystallization occurs when the floating charge becomes a fixed charge on all the assets available on that date - for instance, when the creditor enforces the security due to breach of the terms and conditions of the floating charge, or the company goes into liquidation; until crystallization, a floating charge remains dormant
options.D: Crystallization refers to the process by which a fixed charge is converted into a floating charge upon the company's request to the charge-holder, the reverse of the correct legal effect

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Crystallization occurs when the floating charge becomes a fixed charge on all the assets available on that date - for instance, when the creditor enforces the security due to breach of the terms and conditions of the floating charge, or the company goes into liquidation; until crystallization, a floating charge remains dormant

A floating charge remains dormant (i.e., the company may freely deal with the charged assets) until it 'crystallizes' - becoming fixed on all the assets available on the date of crystallization. This occurs on enforcement of the security by the creditor due to breach, or when the company ceases business, or on liquidation, or when creditors enforce the security covered by the floating charge.

question_html: Which of the following is correctly recognised as an event that may trigger crystallization of a floating charge?

options.A: The mere passage of five years from the date of creation of the floating charge, regardless of whether any default, cessation of business, or liquidation has occurred
options.B: The company obtaining a fresh unsecured loan from any third party, even where such a loan has no connection whatsoever to the floating charge or the assets covered by it
options.C: The company changing its registered office from one state to another, this being treated as an automatic trigger for crystallization under the Companies Act, 2013
options.D: Violation of the terms and conditions of the floating charge (such as non-payment of interest or default in instalments), the company ceasing to continue its business, the company going into liquidation, or the creditors enforcing the security covered by the floating charge

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Violation of the terms and conditions of the floating charge (such as non-payment of interest or default in instalments), the company ceasing to continue its business, the company going into liquidation, or the creditors enforcing the security covered by the floating charge

Crystallization of a floating charge may occur where the terms and conditions of the floating charge are violated (e.g., non-payment of interest, default in instalments), the company ceases to continue its business, the company goes into liquidation, or the creditors enforce the security covered by the floating charge - as illustrated by the Prism Limited example (failure to repay/liquidation converting a floating charge on stock into a fixed charge).

question_html: Once a floating charge has crystallised into a fixed charge, can the company continue to sell or use the previously 'floating' assets (e.g., stock) in its business operations, as it could before crystallization?

options.A: No - once crystallised, the security (raw material, stock-in-trade, etc.) becomes fixed and is available for realisation by the lender so that the borrowed money is repaid; the stock can neither be sold nor used by the company in its business operations thereafter
options.B: Yes - crystallization has no effect at all on the company's freedom to deal with the assets; the assets remain freely saleable and usable exactly as before crystallization occurred
options.C: Yes, but only to the extent of 50% of the crystallised assets, this being a statutory carve-out preserving partial business continuity for the company
options.D: No, but only for a grace period of 90 days after crystallization, after which the company regains full freedom to sell or use the assets notwithstanding the crystallised charge

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - once crystallised, the security (raw material, stock-in-trade, etc.) becomes fixed and is available for realisation by the lender so that the borrowed money is repaid; the stock can neither be sold nor used by the company in its business operations thereafter

Once a floating charge crystallises (becomes fixed), the security is locked in and made available for realisation by the lender to recover the borrowed money - the company loses its earlier freedom to sell or use those assets in the ordinary course of business, exactly as with an ordinary fixed charge, as illustrated by the Prism Limited example.

question_html: Under section 77, whose primary duty is it to register the particulars of a charge created by the company, and does this duty extend to charges on property situated outside India?

options.A: It is exclusively the duty of the lender (charge-holder), and never the company, to register the particulars of any charge created on the company's property, regardless of where the property is situated
options.B: It is the duty of the company creating the charge (within or outside India, on its property/assets/undertakings, whether tangible or otherwise, and whether situated in or outside India) to register the particulars of the charge - the duty extends to charges created on property situated outside India as well
options.C: The duty to register a charge applies only where the charged property is situated within India; charges created on property situated outside India are entirely outside the scope of section 77
options.D: It is the duty of the Registrar of Companies (acting suo motu, without any application from either the company or the charge-holder) to register every charge created by a company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) It is the duty of the company creating the charge (within or outside India, on its property/assets/undertakings, whether tangible or otherwise, and whether situated in or outside India) to register the particulars of the charge - the duty extends to charges created on property situated outside India as well

Section 77 places the primary duty of registration on the company creating the charge, whether the charge is created within or outside India, on tangible or intangible property/assets/undertakings, situated within India or outside India - the location of the charged property does not exempt the company from this duty, as confirmed by the Moon Light Ltd. and Vital Pharmacy illustrations in the Study Material.

question_html: If the company creating a charge fails to register it within the prescribed period of 30 days, what alternative route is available, and to whom?

options.A: No alternative route is available at all; if the company fails to register the charge within 30 days, the charge is permanently and irretrievably void, with no possibility of registration by any person thereafter
options.B: Only the Central Government (and not the charge-holder) may apply to have the charge registered where the company has defaulted in registering it within 30 days

question_html: What must accompany a company's application to the Registrar seeking an extension of time for registration of a charge, and what must the Registrar be satisfied of before allowing such extension?

options.A: The application (in Form CHG-1 for other than debentures, or Form CHG-9 for debentures) must be supported by a declaration, signed by the company's company secretary or a director, that such belated filing shall not adversely affect the rights of any other intervening creditors of the company; and the Registrar must be satisfied that the company had sufficient cause for not filing the particulars/instrument within the original 30-day period, before allowing the extension (and requisite additional/ad valorem fee must be paid)
options.B: The application must be supported by an affidavit from an independent chartered accountant confirming the company's solvency, with no requirement for any declaration regarding the rights of intervening creditors
options.C: No supporting declaration or Registrar satisfaction is required at all; extension of the time limit for registration of a charge is granted automatically upon the mere filing of the application in the prescribed form
options.D: The application must be supported by a special resolution of the shareholders passed in general meeting, in lieu of any declaration by the company secretary or a director

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The application (in Form CHG-1 for other than debentures, or Form CHG-9 for debentures) must be supported by a declaration, signed by the company's company secretary or a director, that such belated filing shall not adversely affect the rights of any other intervening creditors of the company; and the Registrar must be satisfied that the company had sufficient cause for not filing the particulars/instrument within the original 30-day period, before allowing the extension (and requisite additional/ad valorem fee must be paid)

question_html: Under section 80, from what date is a person acquiring property, assets, an undertaking (or part thereof), or any share or interest therein, deemed to have notice of a charge registered under section 77?

question_html: What does 'constructive notice' mean in this context, and what is its practical effect if a person enters into a transaction without checking the register of charges and later suffers loss because of an unnoticed charge?

options.A: 'Constructive notice' means the company must give the acquirer explicit, actual written notice of the charge; if the company fails to do so, the acquirer can freely claim any resulting loss from the company
options.B: 'Constructive' means implied or deemed, and 'notice' means knowledge - so constructive notice means implied/deemed knowledge; even though the person did not actually refer to the register (a public document), he is deemed to have seen it (a legal fiction), and consequently he CANNOT claim the resulting loss from the company, since he is deemed to have had notice of the charge
options.C: 'Constructive notice' has no legal consequence at all for a person who fails to check the register of charges; such a person retains a full claim against the company for any resulting loss regardless of the charge's registration
options.D: 'Constructive notice' applies only to charges created within the preceding 12 months; a charge older than 12 months does not carry constructive notice, and a resulting loss remains claimable from the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) 'Constructive' means implied or deemed, and 'notice' means knowledge - so constructive notice means implied/deemed knowledge; even though the person did not actually refer to the register (a public document), he is deemed to have seen it (a legal fiction), and consequently he CANNOT claim the resulting loss from the company, since he is deemed to have had notice of the charge

Constructive notice ('implied or deemed knowledge') means that even though a third party has not actually referred to the public document (the register of charges), the law deems him to have seen it - a legal fiction created by the deeming provision in section 80. The practical consequence is that if he suffers loss from an unnoticed charge after entering a transaction without due diligence, he cannot claim that loss from the company, since he is deemed to have had notice of the charge (as illustrated by the Vishnu Marketing/Neeraj example).

question_html: Besides giving third parties constructive notice, what additional protective function does compulsory registration of charges serve?

options.A: It serves solely a revenue-generation function for the Central Government through the collection of registration fees, with no protective function for lenders or subsequent purchasers at all
options.B: It serves solely to enable the company's own management to keep internal accounting records, with no external protective function for third parties dealing with the company
options.C: It acts as a method of preventing a company from offering the same assets as security to borrow funds fraudulently from a different lender, since any prospective lender/buyer can check the public register before dealing with the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) It acts as a method of preventing a company from offering the same assets as security to borrow funds fraudulently from a different lender, since any prospective lender/buyer can check the public register before dealing with the company

Because registered charges are public documents searchable on the MCA Portal, compulsory registration allows any prospective lender or buyer to check whether an asset is already charged before dealing with the company - this transparency function also acts as a safeguard against a company fraudulently offering the same asset as security to multiple lenders without their knowledge.

question_html: Under section 77(3), what is the consequence for a charge created by a company that is not duly registered (with a certificate of registration issued by the Registrar)?

options.A: The charge remains fully valid and enforceable against the liquidator and all other creditors, exactly as if it had been duly registered, since section 77(3) applies only to charges created after the commencement of winding-up proceedings
options.B: The charge becomes void against the company itself (extinguishing the underlying debt entirely), though it remains fully enforceable against the liquidator and all other creditors
options.C: The charge is automatically converted into a floating charge (regardless of whether it was originally fixed or floating) if not duly registered, and remains fully enforceable in that converted form against the liquidator
options.D: No such charge shall be taken into account by the liquidator (appointed under the Companies Act, 2013 or the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016) or by any other creditor, unless it is duly registered and a certificate of registration of such charge is given by the Registrar - in effect, the charge becomes void against the liquidator and other creditors, reducing that creditor to the level of an unsecured creditor

answer_html:

question_html: Does the invalidity of an unregistered charge under section 77(3) also invalidate the underlying contract or obligation for repayment of the money secured by that charge?

options.A: No - section 77(4) clarifies that non-registration shall not prejudice any contract or obligation for the repayment of the money secured by the charge; the debt remains valid and may still be enforced against the company through the courts by filing a suit, though the SECURITY is lost
options.B: Yes - non-registration of the charge automatically extinguishes the underlying debt in its entirety, leaving the erstwhile lender with no remedy of any kind against the company
options.C: No, but only where the debt is below rupees ten lakh; for larger debts, non-registration of the charge does extinguish the underlying obligation to repay under section 77(4)
options.D: Yes - the debt is converted, by operation of section 77(4), from a contractual obligation into a purely equitable claim enforceable only through arbitration, and never through the ordinary courts

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - section 77(4) clarifies that non-registration shall not prejudice any contract or obligation for the repayment of the money secured by the charge; the debt remains valid and may still be enforced against the company through the courts by filing a suit, though the SECURITY is lost

Section 77(4) preserves the validity of the underlying contract/obligation to repay the money secured by the charge, notwithstanding non-registration under section 77(3) - the debt remains valid and enforceable via an ordinary suit in court; it is only the SECURITY (the charge itself, and the priority/proprietary protection it confers) that is lost, not the debt.

question_html: Where a company delays registering a charge (registering it only within an extended period rather than the original 30 days), and a second lender obtains and promptly registers a charge on the same property in the meantime, what is the effect on priority between the two charge-holders?

options.A: The first lender always retains priority over the second lender purely on the basis that its charge was created earlier in time, regardless of the relative dates of actual registration of the two charges
options.B: Any subsequent registration of the first charge (even within the extended period) shall not prejudice any right acquired in respect of the property before that first charge is actually registered - so the second lender, having registered promptly, obtains priority over the first lender, even though the first lender's charge was created earlier in time
options.C: Priority between the two lenders is determined by drawing lots between them, since the Companies Act, 2013 provides no substantive priority rule in a case of delayed registration by one of two competing charge-holders
options.D: Both charges are treated as void in their entirety in such a case, with neither lender obtaining any priority or right to recovery from the charged property

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Any subsequent registration of the first charge (even within the extended period) shall not prejudice any right acquired in respect of the property before that first charge is actually registered - so the second lender, having registered promptly, obtains priority over the first lender, even though the first lender's charge was created earlier in time

The Third Proviso to section 77(1) provides that subsequent registration of a charge (even if made within the extended period rather than the original 30 days) shall not prejudice any right acquired in respect of the property BEFORE the charge is actually registered. As illustrated by the Vasudha Medicos Limited example (Bank A's earlier-created but late-registered charge vs. Bank B's later-created but promptly-registered charge), the promptly-registering lender (Bank B) gets priority over the earlier lender (Bank A) whose registration was delayed.

question_html: If the company fails to register the charge within 30 days, and the charge-holder applies to the Registrar under section 78, what is the Registrar's next step, and within what time does registration follow if no objection is received?

options.A: The Registrar shall register the charge immediately upon receipt of the charge-holder's application, without giving any notice to the company at all, and without any opportunity for the company to object
options.B: The Registrar shall reject the charge-holder's application outright in every case, since only the company (and never the charge-holder) has the legal capacity to apply for registration of a charge under section 78
options.C: On receipt of the charge-holder's application, the Registrar shall give a notice to the company; if no objection is received (from the company), the Registrar shall allow such registration, on payment of the prescribed fees, within a period of 14 days after giving notice to the company

Under section 78, upon the charge-holder's application, the Registrar gives notice to the company; if no objection is received (or the company does not itself register the charge, or shows no sufficient cause against registration), the Registrar allows registration, on payment of prescribed fees, within 14 days after giving notice to the company.

subject: Corporate and Other Laws
question_html: In what circumstance will the Registrar decline to allow registration of the charge pursuant to the charge-holder's application under section 78?

options.A: Where the charge-holder is a bank rather than a non-banking financial institution, this distinction alone being sufficient for the Registrar to decline the application regardless of the company's conduct
options.B: Where the amount of the loan secured by the charge exceeds rupees one crore, this monetary threshold alone being sufficient for the Registrar to decline the charge-holder's application
options.C: Where the charge was created more than six months before the charge-holder's application, this time-lapse alone being sufficient for the Registrar to decline the application under section 78
options.D: Where the company itself registers the charge (before the Registrar acts on the charge-holder's application), or the company shows sufficient cause why such charge should not be registered

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Where the company itself registers the charge (before the Registrar acts on the charge-holder's application), or the company shows sufficient cause why such charge should not be registered

The Registrar will not allow registration by the charge-holder if the company itself registers the charge (rendering the charge-holder's application unnecessary), or if the company shows sufficient cause why the charge should not be registered - these are the two recognised grounds on which the Registrar declines to proceed on the charge-holder's section 78 application.

question_html: Where registration of a charge is effected pursuant to an application made by the charge-holder (rather than the company) under section 78, can the charge-holder recover the fees paid for such registration?

options.A: Yes - such person (the charge-holder) shall be entitled to recover from the company the amount of any fees or additional fees paid by him to the Registrar for the purpose of registration of the charge
options.B: No - the charge-holder must bear the entire cost of registration fees permanently, with no right of recovery from the company under any provision of the Companies Act, 2013
options.C: Yes, but only up to 50% of the fees paid, the remaining 50% being treated as the charge-holder's own cost of enforcing its security interest
options.D: No - the charge-holder may only recover such fees by initiating a separate civil suit for damages against the company, since the Companies Act, 2013 itself confers no direct statutory right of recovery

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - such person (the charge-holder) shall be entitled to recover from the company the amount of any fees or additional fees paid by him to the Registrar for the purpose of registration of the charge

Where registration is effected on an application made by the charge-holder (because the company defaulted in registering the charge itself), the charge-holder is statutorily entitled to recover from the company the amount of any fees or additional fees it paid to the Registrar for the purpose of that registration.

question_html: Under section 79(b), what does 'modification' of a charge include, and does a change in the rate of interest on the secured loan amount to a modification requiring fresh registration?

options.A: 'Modification' is confined strictly to a complete replacement of the original charge instrument with an entirely new instrument; a mere change in the rate of interest never qualifies as a 'modification' requiring registration
options.B: 'Modification' includes variation in any of the terms and conditions of the agreement, including a change in the rate of interest (whether by mutual agreement or by operation of law), as well as variation in the extent or operation of the charge - and even assignment of the charge-holder's rights to a third party is regarded as a modification
options.C: 'Modification' under section 79(b) applies only to a change in the identity of the charge-holder by way of a fresh charge, and never to a change in the rate of interest or the extent/operation of the existing charge
options.D: 'Modification' is confined strictly to an increase (and never a decrease) in the credit limits secured by the charge; a decrease in limits is treated as a fresh, independent charge rather than a modification

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) 'Modification' includes variation in any of the terms and conditions of the agreement, including a change in the rate of interest (whether by mutual agreement or by operation of law), as well as variation in the extent or operation of the charge - and even assignment of the charge-holder's rights to a third party is regarded as a modification

Section 79(b) requires any modification in charge - a change in terms and conditions, extent, or operation, INCLUDING a change in the rate of interest (by mutual agreement or operation of law) - to be registered by the company in accordance with section 77. Even an assignment of the charge-holder's rights to a third party is regarded as a modification requiring registration.

question_html: Which of the following is correctly recognised as an example of 'modification of charge'?

options.A: Only a complete cancellation of the entire charge is recognised as a 'modification'; partial release of the charge on a specific asset is treated as a wholly separate, unrelated legal event outside the scope of section 79(b)
options.B: Only a change in the identity of the company (through a merger or amalgamation) is recognised as a 'modification'; changes to interest rates, credit limits, or repayment schedules are excluded from the concept entirely
options.C: Modification by ceding a pari passu charge (where the original charge-holder becomes a second charge-holder, subject to full satisfaction of the first charge-holder's claim), an agreement enhancing or decreasing credit limits, a change in the repayment schedule of a loan (not applicable to working loans repayable on demand), and partial release of the charge on a particular asset
options.D: Only an increase (never a decrease) in the credit limits secured by a charge is recognised as a 'modification'; any decrease is instead treated as an automatic, unregistrable partial satisfaction of the charge

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Modification by ceding a pari passu charge (where the original charge-holder becomes a second charge-holder, subject to full satisfaction of the first charge-holder's claim), an agreement enhancing or decreasing credit limits, a change in the repayment schedule of a loan (not applicable to working loans repayable on demand), and partial release of the charge on a particular asset

The Study Material lists several illustrative examples of 'modification of charge': varying terms/conditions by agreement, enhancing/decreasing credit limits, ceding a pari passu charge (making the original holder a second charge-holder, ranking after full satisfaction of the first holder's claim), a change in repayment schedule (excluding working loans repayable on demand), and partial release of the charge on a particular asset/property.

question_html: Under section 79(a), where a company acquires property on which a charge is already registered (with the permission of the charge-holder), what is that acquiring company's duty?

options.A: The acquiring company has no duty to register anything, since the pre-existing registration in the seller's name continues to apply automatically to the new owner without any fresh action
options.B: The acquiring company's sole duty is to notify the original seller (not the Registrar) of the change in ownership, with no independent registration obligation of its own under section 79(a)
options.C: The acquiring company's duty is discharged by simply continuing to make loan repayments to the charge-holder on the seller's behalf, without any requirement of registering the charge afresh in its own name
options.D: It shall be the duty of the company acquiring the property to get the charge registered in accordance with section 77 - in effect, the earlier charge should get vacated, and, in its place, a new charge should get registered by the company that has now acquired the property

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) It shall be the duty of the company acquiring the property to get the charge registered in accordance with section 77 - in effect, the earlier charge should get vacated, and, in its place, a new charge should get registered by the company that has now acquired the property

Section 79(a) requires a company acquiring property already subject to a registered charge (sold with the charge-holder's permission) to get the charge registered afresh, in its own name, in accordance with section 77 - the earlier (seller's) registration should be vacated and replaced by a fresh registration in the acquiring company's name.

question_html: Under section 81(1), what must the Registrar keep in respect of every company, and what does Rule 7(1) deem to constitute this register for the purposes of section 81?

options.A: The Registrar shall keep a register containing particulars of the charges registered under Chapter VI, in the prescribed form and manner; Rule 7(1) deems the particulars of charges maintained on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal (www.mca.gov.in/MCA21) to be the register of charges for the purposes of section 81
options.B: The Registrar has no obligation to maintain any register of charges at all; the obligation to maintain such a register rests solely and exclusively with each individual company under section 85
options.C: Rule 7(1) deems the particulars of charges maintained in each company's own internal physical records (and not the MCA portal) to be the register of charges for the purposes of section 81
options.D: The Registrar's register under section 81 is confined to charges registered by public companies; charges registered by private companies are excluded from the Registrar's register altogether

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) The Registrar shall keep a register containing particulars of the charges registered under Chapter VI, in the prescribed form and manner; Rule 7(1) deems the particulars of charges maintained on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal (www.mca.gov.in/MCA21) to be the register of charges for the purposes of section 81

Section 81(1) requires the Registrar to keep, for every company, a register of particulars of charges registered under Chapter VI. Rule 7(1) provides that the particulars of charges maintained on the MCA Portal (www.mca.gov.in/MCA21) shall be deemed to be this register - i.e., the Registrar's statutory register is, in practice, the electronic record on the MCA Portal, not a separate physical register.

question_html: Under section 85(1) and Rule 10(1), what must every company keep at its registered office, in what form, and what must it include?

options.A: Every company shall keep a Register of Charges only at the office of the Registrar of Companies (not at its own registered office), and the Register need include only fixed charges, expressly excluding floating charges
options.B: Every company shall keep a Register of Charges (in Form CHG-7, per Rule 10(1)) in the prescribed form and manner at its registered office; the Register shall include all charges AND floating charges affecting any property or assets of the company (or any of its undertakings), indicating the prescribed particulars in each case; a copy of the instrument creating the charge must also be kept along with the Register
options.C: Every company shall keep a Register of Charges in Form CHG-1, and this Register need not include any copy of the instrument creating the charge, since that instrument is filed separately only with the Registrar
options.D: No company has any independent obligation to keep its own Register of Charges; reliance on the Registrar's MCA-Portal-based register under section 81 is treated as full compliance for every company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Every company shall keep a Register of Charges (in Form CHG-7, per Rule 10(1)) in the prescribed form and manner at its registered office; the Register shall include all charges AND floating charges affecting any property or assets of the company (or any of its undertakings), indicating the prescribed particulars in each case; a copy of the instrument creating the charge must also be kept along with the Register

Section 85(1) (read with Rule 10(1), specifying Form CHG-7) requires every company to keep, at its OWN registered office, a Register of Charges including all charges and floating charges affecting its property/assets/undertakings, with prescribed particulars in each case - and the proviso to section 85(1) requires a copy of the instrument creating the charge to be kept alongside the Register.

question_html: Under section 85(2) and Rule 10(4), who may inspect the company's Register of Charges without paying a fee, and for how long must the Register (and the instrument creating a charge) be preserved?

options.A: Only the company's own directors may inspect the Register of Charges, and no member, creditor, or other person has any right of inspection at all, whether or not a fee is paid
options.B: Every person, whether or not a member or creditor of the company, may inspect the Register of Charges and the instrument of charges entirely free of charge, with no distinction in treatment between categories of persons
options.C: Any member or creditor of the company may inspect the Register of Charges and the instrument of charges, during business hours, without payment of any fee (any other person may inspect only on payment of prescribed fees, subject to reasonable restrictions the company may impose by its articles); the Register itself shall be preserved permanently, while the instrument creating a charge (or its modification) shall be preserved for a period of eight years from the date of satisfaction of the charge
options.D: The Register of Charges (and the instrument creating a charge) must be destroyed within three years of the satisfaction of the relevant charge, in the interest of minimising the company's document-retention burden

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Any member or creditor of the company may inspect the Register of Charges and the instrument of charges, during business hours, without payment of any fee (any other person may inspect only on payment of prescribed fees, subject to reasonable restrictions the company may impose by its articles); the Register itself shall be preserved permanently, while the instrument creating a charge (or its modification) shall be preserved for a period of eight years from the date of satisfaction of the charge

Section 85(2) grants members and creditors fee-free inspection of the Register of Charges and instrument of charges during business hours; any other person may inspect only on payment of the prescribed fee, subject to reasonable restrictions the company may impose by its articles (Rule 11 mirrors this). Rule 10(4) requires the Register itself to be preserved PERMANENTLY, while the instrument creating a charge (or its modification) need be preserved only for EIGHT YEARS from the date of satisfaction of the charge.

question_html: Under section 82, within what period must a company give intimation to the Registrar of payment or satisfaction in full of a registered charge, and to what extent may this period be extended?

options.A: The company must give intimation within 90 days from the date of payment or satisfaction, with no provision at all for any further extension of this period under section 82
options.B: The company must give intimation within 7 days from the date of payment or satisfaction, and this period may be extended to a maximum of 60 days only, on payment of ad valorem fees
options.C: There is no fixed timeline at all for intimation of satisfaction of charge under section 82; the company may give such intimation to the Registrar at any time it considers convenient
options.D: The company must give intimation within 30 days from the date of such payment or satisfaction; the proviso to section 82(1) allows the Registrar, on an application by the company or the charge-holder, to extend this period up to 300 days from the date of payment/satisfaction, on payment of prescribed additional fees

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) The company must give intimation within 30 days from the date of such payment or satisfaction; the proviso to section 82(1) allows the Registrar, on an application by the company or the charge-holder, to extend this period up to 300 days from the date of payment/satisfaction, on payment of prescribed additional fees

Section 82(1) requires intimation of full payment/satisfaction of a registered charge within 30 days of such payment/satisfaction; the proviso extends this to up to 300 days (on application by the company OR the charge-holder), on payment of prescribed additional fees - Rule 8(1) having been amended in 2018 to substitute this 300-day period in place of the earlier 30-day-only regime.

subject: Corporate and Other Laws
question_html: Under section 83, can the Registrar make an entry as to satisfaction/release of a registered charge even where NO intimation has been received from the company?

options.A: Yes - section 83 empowers the Registrar to make entries with respect to satisfaction and release of charges even if no intimation has been received from the company, provided evidence is shown to the Registrar's satisfaction that the debt has been paid/satisfied wholly or in part, or that the charged property has been released from the charge or has ceased to form part of the company's property; the Registrar must inform the affected parties within 30 days of making such an entry
options.B: No - the Registrar has no power at all to record satisfaction of a charge without formal intimation from the company; the company's intimation is an indispensable precondition under all circumstances
options.C: Yes, but only where the intimation is instead received from the charge-holder; section 83 does not empower the Registrar to act on evidence from any other source, such as a third-party purchaser
options.D: No - section 83 empowers only the National Company Law Tribunal (and not the Registrar) to record satisfaction of a charge in the absence of intimation from the company

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Yes - section 83 empowers the Registrar to make entries with respect to satisfaction and release of charges even if no intimation has been received from the company, provided evidence is shown to the Registrar's satisfaction that the debt has been paid/satisfied wholly or in part, or that the charged property has been released from the charge or has ceased to form part of the company's property; the Registrar must inform the affected parties within 30 days of making such an entry

Before the default and liquidation, could Meridian Ceramics Limited have sold its factory land and building (subject to the fixed charge) without reference to Coastal Commercial Bank?

options.A: The floating charge crystallises - it becomes a fixed charge on all the inventory (raw material and finished goods) available on the date of crystallization; the company can thereafter neither sell nor use that inventory in its business operations, and it becomes available for realisation by the bank to recover the outstanding loan

question_html:
Harbourline Logistics Limited created a charge on its warehouse property in favour of Falcon Finance Ltd. on 3rd January, 2026, but did not register this charge within the original 30-day period. Subsequently, on 20th February, 2026, Harbourline Logistics created a second charge on the SAME warehouse property in favour of Meadowbrook Capital Ltd., which Meadowbrook Capital promptly and duly registered on 26th February, 2026. Falcon Finance's charge was only registered later, on 15th April, 2026 (within the permissible extended period, after payment of the requisite additional fees and demonstration of sufficient cause). Harbourline Logistics subsequently went into liquidation, and the warehouse property realised an amount sufficient to repay only one of the two lenders in full.

As between Falcon Finance Ltd. (charge created 3rd January, 2026, registered 15th April, 2026) and Meadowbrook Capital Ltd. (charge created 20th February, 2026, registered 26th February, 2026), which lender gets priority in repayment from the warehouse property's realised value?

options.A: Meadowbrook Capital Ltd. gets priority - even though its charge was created LATER in time (20th February, 2026, as against Falcon Finance's 3rd January, 2026), it registered its charge promptly and BEFORE Falcon Finance actually registered its own charge (15th April, 2026); the Third Proviso to section 77(1) provides that subsequent registration of Falcon Finance's charge (albeit within the permissible extended period) shall not prejudice the right Meadowbrook Capital acquired before Falcon Finance's charge was actually registered
options.B: Falcon Finance Ltd. gets priority, purely because its charge was created earlier in time (3rd January, 2026), regardless of the fact that its registration was delayed until 15th April, 2026, well after Meadowbrook Capital's charge was both created and registered
options.C: Neither lender gets any priority over the other; the realised sum must be shared strictly pro rata between Falcon Finance and Meadowbrook Capital in proportion to their respective loan amounts, irrespective of registration dates
options.D: Falcon Finance Ltd. gets priority because it registered its charge within the permissible extended period allowed under the Second Proviso to section 77(1), which is deemed to relate back to the original date of creation of its charge for all purposes

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) Meadowbrook Capital Ltd. gets priority - even though its charge was created LATER in time (20th February, 2026, as against Falcon Finance's 3rd January, 2026), it registered its charge promptly and BEFORE Falcon Finance actually registered its own charge (15th April, 2026); the Third Proviso to section 77(1) provides that subsequent registration of Falcon Finance's charge (albeit within the permissible extended period) shall not prejudice the right Meadowbrook Capital acquired before Falcon Finance's charge was actually registered

This scenario mirrors the Vasudha Medicos Limited illustration in the Study Material: the Third Proviso to section 77(1) provides that subsequent registration of a delayed charge (even within the extended period) does not prejudice rights acquired in the property before that charge was actually registered. Meadowbrook Capital's charge, though created later, was registered on 26th February 2026 - before Falcon Finance actually registered its charge on 15th April 2026 - so Meadowbrook Capital acquired its right first in point of actual registration, and thus gets priority over Falcon Finance.

Assuming the realised warehouse proceeds are entirely exhausted in repaying Meadowbrook Capital Ltd., does Falcon Finance Ltd. lose its entire claim against Harbourline Logistics Limited, including the underlying debt itself?

options.A: Yes - Falcon Finance loses its entire claim in full, both as to the security and as to the underlying debt itself, since section 77(4) applies only to charges that were registered on time, not to charges (like Falcon Finance's) that were registered late
options.B: No - although Falcon Finance loses its SECURITY (and its priority claim on the specific warehouse property, given Meadowbrook Capital's superior claim), section 77(4) preserves the validity of the underlying contract/obligation for repayment; Falcon Finance's debt remains valid and may still be pursued against Harbourline Logistics (now in liquidation) as an unsecured claim, through the ordinary insolvency/winding-up process
options.C: No - Falcon Finance actually retains full priority over Meadowbrook Capital in respect of the underlying debt (though not the specific security), since a debt obligation always outranks a mere secured charge under section 77(4)
options.D: Yes - Falcon Finance's underlying debt is automatically extinguished the moment a competing, promptly-registered charge is found to have priority over it, regardless of section 77(4)

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) No - although Falcon Finance loses its SECURITY (and its priority claim on the specific warehouse property, given Meadowbrook Capital's superior claim), section 77(4) preserves the validity of the underlying contract/obligation for repayment; Falcon Finance's debt remains valid and may still be pursued against Harbourline Logistics (now in liquidation) as an unsecured claim, through the ordinary insolvency/winding-up process

Section 77(4) confirms that non-registration (or delayed registration resulting in loss of priority) does not prejudice the underlying contract or obligation for repayment of the secured money - the debt survives and remains enforceable, but merely as an unsecured claim (given Falcon Finance's loss of security/priority on this specific property), rather than as a claim ranking ahead of, or equally with, Meadowbrook Capital's properly-prioritised secured claim.

Suppose, hypothetically, that Falcon Finance Ltd. had never registered its charge at all (not even within the extended period) before Harbourline Logistics Limited's liquidation. What would be the effect on Falcon Finance's position in the liquidation, per section 77(3)?

options.A: The unregistered charge would still be fully recognised by the liquidator and would rank equally with Meadowbrook Capital's duly registered charge, since both charges relate to genuine, bona fide loans advanced to Harbourline Logistics
options.B: The unregistered charge would automatically take priority over Meadowbrook Capital's registered charge in the liquidation, as a penalty imposed on Meadowbrook Capital for having registered so promptly
options.C: The unregistered charge would not be taken into account by the liquidator at all - it would, in effect, be void against the liquidator (and against Meadowbrook Capital and other creditors), and Falcon Finance would be reduced to the position of an unsecured creditor in the liquidation, ranking behind Meadowbrook Capital's duly registered and prioritised secured claim
options.D: The liquidator would be statutorily barred from recognising ANY charge on the warehouse property (registered or unregistered) once liquidation commences, so neither Falcon Finance nor Meadowbrook Capital could claim as a secured creditor

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) The unregistered charge would not be taken into account by the liquidator at all - it would, in effect, be void against the liquidator (and against Meadowbrook Capital and other creditors), and Falcon Finance would be reduced to the position of an unsecured creditor in the liquidation, ranking behind Meadowbrook Capital's duly registered and prioritised secured claim

Section 77(3) provides that no charge shall be taken into account by the liquidator (or any other creditor) unless it is duly registered with a Registrar's certificate - a wholly unregistered charge is void against the liquidator and other creditors at winding up, reducing that charge-holder (here, Falcon Finance, in this hypothetical) to unsecured-creditor status, ranking behind Meadowbrook Capital's validly registered and prioritised secured claim.

Two years later, Kestrel Developers sold this building to Mr. Arvind, a real estate investor, without informing him of the existing registered charge. Mr. Arvind did not check the register of charges maintained by the Registrar of Companies (or the MCA Portal) before completing the purchase. After the sale, Kestrel Developers defaulted on its loan, and Northbridge Capital sought to enforce its charge against the building now owned by Mr. Arvind. question_html:
Kestrel Developers Limited created and duly registered a charge on its commercial building in Pune in favour of Northbridge Capital, securing a loan of Rs. 4 crore. Two years later, Kestrel Developers sold this building to Mr. Arvind, a real estate investor, without informing him of the existing registered charge. Mr. Arvind did not check the register of charges maintained by the Registrar of Companies (or the MCA Portal) before completing the purchase. After the sale, Kestrel Developers defaulted on its loan, and Northbridge Capital sought to enforce its charge against the building now owned by Mr. Arvind. Mr. Arvind protested that he had no actual knowledge of the charge and sought to recover his resulting loss from Kestrel Developers.

Is Mr. Arvind deemed to have had notice of Northbridge Capital's registered charge on the building, even though he never actually checked the register of charges before purchasing it?

options.A: No - deemed notice under section 80 applies only where the acquirer actually inspects the register of charges and fails to notice the entry due to his own negligence; an acquirer who never inspects the register at all is entirely exempt from constructive notice
options.B: No - since Kestrel Developers did not affirmatively inform Mr. Arvind of the charge, section 80 does not apply, and Mr. Arvind is treated as having no notice of the charge whatsoever, whether actual or constructive
options.C: Yes, but only if Mr. Arvind is found to be a real estate professional by occupation; an ordinary individual purchaser without professional real estate expertise would not be deemed to have notice under section 80
options.D: Yes - under section 80, since the charge was registered under section 77, Mr. Arvind (as a person acquiring the charged property) is DEEMED to have notice of the charge from the date of its registration, regardless of whether he actually inspected the register; this is a legal fiction (constructive notice) that does not depend on his actual, subjective knowledge

answer_html:
Correct answer: (D) Yes - under section 80, since the charge was registered under section 77, Mr. Arvind (as a person acquiring the charged property) is DEEMED to have notice of the charge from the date of its registration, regardless of whether he actually inspected the register; this is a legal fiction (constructive notice) that does not depend on his actual, subjective knowledge

Section 80 creates a legal fiction: any person acquiring property on which a charge is registered under section 77 is deemed to have notice of the charge from the date of registration - irrespective of whether that person actually inspected the public register, and irrespective of the acquirer's profession or expertise. This mirrors the Vishnu Marketing Limited/Neeraj illustration in the Study Material.

Mr. Arvind protested that he had no actual knowledge of the charge and sought to recover his resulting loss from Kestrel Developers.

Can Mr. Arvind successfully recover his resulting loss (arising from Northbridge Capital's enforcement of the charge) from Kestrel Developers Limited, on the ground that he was not actually told about the charge?

options.A: No - because Mr. Arvind is deemed, under section 80, to have had notice of the registered charge from the date of its registration, he cannot plead lack of actual knowledge to claim the resulting loss from Kestrel Developers; he ought to have verified the register of charges before completing the purchase
options.B: Yes - since Kestrel Developers failed to affirmatively disclose the charge to Mr. Arvind at the time of sale, he can recover his full loss from the company notwithstanding section 80's deeming provision
options.C: Yes - deemed notice under section 80 protects only the charge-holder (Northbridge Capital) against the company, and confers no protection at all on the company (Kestrel Developers) against a claim by the purchaser
options.D: No, but only because Mr. Arvind is a real estate investor by profession; had he been an ordinary individual buyer, he would have retained a valid claim against Kestrel Developers for his loss

answer_html:
Correct answer: (A) No - because Mr. Arvind is deemed, under section 80, to have had notice of the registered charge from the date of its registration, he cannot plead lack of actual knowledge to claim the resulting loss from Kestrel Developers; he ought to have verified the register of charges before completing the purchase

As with the Vishnu Marketing Limited/Neeraj example, once a person is deemed (under section 80) to have had notice of a registered charge from its date of registration, he cannot plead ignorance to claim any resulting loss from the company - the deeming provision operates as a complete answer to such a claim, precisely because compulsory registration exists to make the charge publicly discoverable in advance of any transaction.

What broader protective function does the compulsory registration of Northbridge Capital's charge serve in a scenario like this one, beyond merely fixing Mr. Arvind with deemed notice?

options.A: It serves no protective function at all beyond fixing individual purchasers with deemed notice; it has no bearing on preventing fraudulent multiple charging of the same asset by the company
options.B: It prevents Kestrel Developers Limited from being able to deal fraudulently with the same asset (e.g., raising a further, undisclosed loan against the same building from a different lender) by ensuring the charge is publicly discoverable on the MCA Portal, so that any prospective purchaser or lender (like Mr. Arvind, had he checked) could verify the building's charge status before transacting
options.C: It exists solely to generate registration-fee revenue for the Registrar of Companies, and has no substantive protective or transparency-related function for third parties such as Mr. Arvind
options.D: It exists solely to protect Northbridge Capital's interests, and confers no corresponding benefit or protective function for prospective purchasers such as Mr. Arvind, who remain wholly unprotected by the registration system

answer_html:

Beyond the immediate deemed-notice consequence for Mr. Arvind, compulsory registration under Chapter VI creates a publicly searchable record (via the MCA Portal) that protects the broader market - preventing a company like Kestrel Developers from fraudulently offering the same asset as security to multiple lenders or misrepresenting its charge-free status to a prospective purchaser, since any diligent party can verify the true position before transacting.

question_html:
Silverline Textiles Limited created a charge on its dyeing unit machinery in favour of Crestwood Capital Ltd., securing a loan of Rs. 2.5 crore, the instrument of charge being duly executed by both parties. Owing to an internal communication lapse, Silverline Textiles failed to register the particulars of this charge with the Registrar within the prescribed period of 30 days from its creation, and continued to remain in default of this registration obligation despite repeated reminders from Crestwood Capital. Crestwood Capital thereafter decided to itself apply to the Registrar for registration of the charge, along with the instrument of charge, in the prescribed form and manner.

Is Crestwood Capital Ltd., as the charge-holder, entitled to apply to the Registrar for registration of the charge, given Silverline Textiles Limited's continuing default in registering it?

options.A: No - only the company itself (and never the charge-holder) has the legal capacity to apply for registration of a charge under the Companies Act, 2013, regardless of how long the company's default continues
options.B: No - Crestwood Capital must first obtain an order from the National Company Law Tribunal directing Silverline Textiles to register the charge, before it can itself apply to the Registrar
options.C: Yes - under section 78, since Silverline Textiles (the company primarily responsible for registration) has failed to register the charge within the prescribed 30-day period, Crestwood Capital, as the person in whose favour the charge is created, may apply to the Registrar for registration of the charge along with the instrument of charge, in the prescribed time, form, and manner
options.D: Yes, but only if Silverline Textiles Limited provides its written consent to Crestwood Capital's application; absent such consent, Crestwood Capital has no independent right to apply under section 78

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - under section 78, since Silverline Textiles (the company primarily responsible for registration) has failed to register the charge within the prescribed 30-day period, Crestwood Capital, as the person in whose favour the charge is created, may apply to the Registrar for registration of the charge along with the instrument of charge, in the prescribed time, form, and manner

Section 78 exists precisely to protect a charge-holder against the company's default in registering a charge - it empowers the charge-holder (here, Crestwood Capital) to apply directly to the Registrar for registration, along with the instrument of charge, once the company fails to do so within the prescribed 30-day period, without requiring any Tribunal order or the defaulting company's consent.

Brightway Foods Limited had earlier created and duly registered a charge on its cold storage facility in favour of Anchor Trade Finance Ltd., securing a working capital loan. Since Brightway Foods Limited missed the original 30-day deadline for intimating satisfaction of the Anchor Trade Finance charge (repaid on 10th January, 2026), can it still validly give such intimation, and within what outer time limit?

options.A: No - once the original 30-day period from the date of repayment has lapsed, Brightway Foods has permanently and irretrievably lost the ability to give intimation of satisfaction under section 82, with no further recourse
options.B: Yes - the proviso to section 82(1) allows the Registrar, on an application by the company (or by the charge-holder, Anchor Trade Finance), to permit intimation of satisfaction within 300 days of the date of payment/satisfaction (i.e., 10th January, 2026), on payment of the prescribed additional fees
options.C: Yes, but only within a further 30 days (i.e., a maximum of 60 days from repayment in total), and only on an application made by Anchor Trade Finance (and never by Brightway Foods itself)
options.D: Yes, but only within a further 15 days (i.e., a maximum of 45 days from repayment in total), and without any requirement to pay additional fees for this extension

answer_html:
Correct answer: (B) Yes - the proviso to section 82(1) allows the Registrar, on an application by the company (or by the charge-holder, Anchor Trade Finance), to permit intimation of satisfaction within 300 days of the date of payment/satisfaction (i.e., 10th January, 2026), on payment of the prescribed additional fees

The proviso to section 82(1) extends the ordinary 30-day intimation period to up to 300 days from the date of payment/satisfaction, on an application by the company OR the charge-holder, and on payment of prescribed additional fees - so Brightway Foods can still validly intimate satisfaction of the Anchor Trade Finance charge, provided it does so within 300 days of 10th January, 2026.

In respect of the OLDER charge (in favour of Solace Credit Co-operative Bank, on the land sold to the third-party buyer several years ago), where neither Brightway Foods nor Solace Credit ever filed particulars of satisfaction, does the buyer have any recourse to get the register corrected, given that he has clear evidence of full repayment from Solace Credit's own records?

options.A: No - since neither Brightway Foods nor Solace Credit ever gave intimation under section 82, the Registrar has no power at all to correct the register in respect of this older charge, regardless of any evidence the buyer may produce
options.B: No - the buyer, not being the company or the charge-holder, has no standing whatsoever to approach the Registrar in respect of this charge; only Brightway Foods or Solace Credit may initiate any correction of the register
options.C: Yes - section 83 empowers the Registrar to make entries with respect to satisfaction and release of a charge even where NO intimation has been received from the company (or the charge-holder); the buyer (or any interested party) can approach the Registrar and show evidence to his satisfaction that the debt secured by the charge has been paid/satisfied, upon which the Registrar may enter a memorandum of satisfaction in the register of charges and must inform affected parties within 30 days of making that entry
options.D: Yes, but only by filing a civil suit against Brightway Foods in the jurisdictional court; section 83 does not empower the Registrar to act directly on evidence produced by a third-party buyer

answer_html:
Correct answer: (C) Yes - section 83 empowers the Registrar to make entries with respect to satisfaction and release of a charge even where NO intimation has been received from the company (or the charge-holder); the buyer (or any interested party) can approach the Registrar and show evidence to his satisfaction that the debt secured by the charge has been paid/satisfied, upon which the Registrar may enter a memorandum of satisfaction in the register of charges and must inform affected parties within 30 days of making that entry

Section 83 is designed precisely for a situation like this - where a charged asset has been sold and satisfaction was never intimated by either the company or the charge-holder - by empowering the Registrar to record a memorandum of satisfaction upon being shown satisfactory evidence (from any source, including a buyer relying on the erstwhile lender's own records) that the debt has been paid; this power exists independently of, and despite, the absence of any intimation under section 82, as confirmed by section 82(4).
